title: Honoring our Ancestors
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of simplicity, humility, and connection with one's ancestors in Zen practice. Drawing inspiration from American Zen teacher Robert Aitken Roshi, Nomon Tim Burnett encourages students to focus on basic practices like breath counting meditation, which cultivates releasing and inquiring, rather than elaborate rituals or intellectual pursuits. By embracing the impermanence of all things and finding freedom in the present moment, we can deepen our practice and connect with a sense of reverence and respect for those who have come before us.

sentences.text: I probably don't remember to say this very often, but it's really quite a privilege for me to get to stand in the center of the circle.
The only reason I can do that is because you're all holding me, so I really appreciate that a lot.
I also want to appreciate Bob for tirelessly keeping this little practice going.
Doesn't it seem like ten years is just enough to start something?
It's like we're learning something about the pace of real change and transformation.
We thought we were starting something twenty years ago, but now we're just starting something now.
It just took twenty years to get started starting.
And it's a pleasure to get to begin the formal practice of our weekend together with some words.
When I was thinking about the talk, of course I thought about the sutra, the essay by Dogen that we'll be chanting as we go along the trail, the Mountains and Rivers Sutra, Sansui Kyo.
I found the mind really wanting to study that again and come up with some pithy things to say about it.
But of course I didn't really have time.
So then I had this strong temptation toward a last-minute cramming session.
And Dogen, if you've ever read Dogen, does not lend himself to cramming.
It's the anti-cramming text.
It's not really crammable.
So I relinquished that desire.
I think we'll learn about Sansui Kyo as we hike.
Instead, I actually want to repeat something that I wrote.
I haven't gotten to say this out loud, but I wrote it in the last [unclear: "Responding Gate"] email newsletter, which some of you maybe have read, and not all of you probably.
I think it bears repeating, and it's very relevant to what we're trying to do.
On August 5th, soon after several of us returned from Japan, where we were on a three-week study immersion trip with colleagues from Everyday Zen, Robert Aitken Roshi died at the age of 93.
I had that wrong before.
I said 83.
Actually, it was 93.
So I give him another ten years.
Aitken Roshi is a really important American Zen teacher, the most important American Zen teacher to date.
But if you say that, it probably pisses somebody off, so I won't say that.
But very important Zen teacher, known for his real care in scholarship and practice.
A very deliberate, very careful practitioner, with a kind of warm devotion.
Warm but uncompromising devotion to formal Zen practice.
He was also well known for social activism.
He didn't feel like Buddhism would be very useful if it was just a hobby for middle class or upper middle class people.
He wanted Buddhist practice to be very relevant and dynamic and immersed in the world.
I was actually thinking about that today at the school bus stop, because our school bus stop is in a pretty low rent neighborhood.
There were three moms there and me.
One mom was from Mexico.
When she first came to the school bus stop, she couldn't speak any English.
But now she has better English than my Spanish, so I've given up trying to talk to her in Spanish.
There's a [unclear: "Lemi"] woman who's there.
And there was a white woman whom I didn't know.
It was clear that none of these three women had very much money.
None of them, I don't think, had gone to college or had the opportunity to go to college.
The woman from [unclear: "Lemi"] told us today that she's the youngest of twelve children.
And just from her demeanor and the way she was talking, you could tell that she'd done fine and she was happy, but life had not been what we would consider very easy for her.
That made me think about what we're doing.
I'd also heard that the Census Bureau, just today, released new statistics on American poverty.
One out of seven people in America are below the federal poverty limit.
And here were three of them.
So anyway, Aitken Roshi cared about these folks, not just the Zen students.
His books and his teaching and his sangha building work have had a huge impact.
Very few American Zen students, I think, have not read at least one of his books.
If you're in that category, you can easily correct that.
We have quite a few at the library.
And through his Japanese teachers, he created an entire school of American Zen, which has been very successful and very popular and very helpful to a lot of people.
I got to meet him one time, and I was really impressed.
His wife had just died a year or so before, after a long marriage.
He was in Seattle to visit with the Seattle group in his lineage and to help Jack Duffy, his student.
I was standing there at the door when he arrived, so I was lucky, I was with Norman.
When he arrived, the sangha members gave him a statue, I'm not sure if it was a Buddhist figure or another kind of statue.
It was a statue of a crying figure, really curled up and really upset.
I didn't get a good look at it, but I had a sense of that intense grief, when you're so upset and so sad that all you can do is curl up.
They gave him that statue as a way of talking about his wife's death.
The way he received it was so graceful and so clear.
He held it up and he looked at it for a few minutes in silence.
Then he said something in such a quiet voice.
And then he went on with what he had to do.
He was there to conduct a big ceremony.
He wasn't there to have a memorial for his wife.
But you could tell that he really received that with an open heart.
I forget all his medical conditions at the end of his life.
I think he had Parkinson's and some other complication.
For the last years he required full-time care.
But all of his students and family organized so that he could stay at the Zen Center in Honolulu, [unclear: "Paolo"] Zen Center in Honolulu, up until about a month before he died.
It said on their website that he continued to do weekly zazen and study and write up until very close to his death.
The other surprising thing about the last years of his life is that he started writing a blog.
He always struck me as an old-school guy, the last guy you'd think of who would write a blog.
He writes books.
It's hard to imagine him even at a computer.
But I read his blog.
He kept it for a couple of years, but it was one short entry every month or two, so it was not that many words.
As such, they speak loudly.
These were the last public things that he said to the world.
So you really have a feeling of things that he thought about carefully and was deliberate in choosing, what to say to all of his students and the rest of the world as he passed away.
One blog post was called "All Things Come."
He wrote:
*Zen practice is a matter of patience.
To quote the proverb, all things come to those who wait.
There are the similar lines at the close of the John Milton sonnet on blindness: They also serve who only stand and wait.
They also serve who only stand and wait.
Similar, but there is a fundamental difference.
It's highlighted with the directionality of "come to" and "serve."
First one, all things come to those who wait.
The second one, they also serve who only stand and wait.*
*As Dogen Zenji said, that the self advances and confirms the myriad things is delusion.
That the myriad things advance and confirm the self is true realization.*
That the self advances and confirms the myriad things is delusion.
That the myriad things advance and confirm the self is true realization.
It makes me think about my urge to cram with the Mountains and Rivers Sutra.
That's the self advancing.
So I appreciated that.
But then there were two posts on a similar theme that really struck me, especially as some of his final teachings to the world.
He did a huge amount of stuff.
As that little section suggests, he was a very learned person, very well read, a very scholarly man, in Western and Eastern philosophy and literature.
Yet these next blog posts really point to the simplicity of practice.
The first one is called "Our Tendency."
He wrote:
*There are two characters in the story, Xue Feng and Xuansha.
Xue Feng called Xuansha a true ascetic.
One day he cornered him and said, "You're a reborn sage.
Why don't you go about on pilgrimage to meet the enlightened masters?"
Xuansha said, "Bodhidharma didn't come to China.
The second ancestor didn't go to India."*
That's some standard Zen lingo.
Then Aitken goes on:
*Xuansha is our true teacher.
We tend to go over here and over there, to Zen and its many stories, to Vipassana, to all kinds of Hindu faiths, to Meister Eckhart and the various saints.
Whatever happened to just counting your breath?
One, two, three, and so on, up to ten.
That is a true pilgrimage.
Xuansha is smiling.
Even Bodhidharma cracks his face.*
Bodhidharma has been very fierce.
He can't smile actually, but his face can crack open.
So that was Xue Feng and Xuansha.
Another post, very short, is just called "Count Your Breaths."
Aitken Roshi wrote:
*If your teacher is not a fake, he or she will tell you to count your breaths.
If he or she advises you to do something else at the onset of your practice, you have a fake teacher.
Use this criterion and find somebody genuine.*
That's pretty direct.
When you read that, if you look at it the wrong way, it sounds sort of narrow and sectarian, maybe.
I don't read it that way.
I read it as deeply appreciating the radical simplicity of what we're trying to do.
If somebody is coaching you to be elaborate and complicated and brilliant, maybe that's not so helpful.
So reading these blog posts and thinking about Aitken Roshi, as I've been thinking about our time in Japan at these ancient temples, I'm thinking about the presence of ancestors.
We hear about ancestor worship as a quaint cultural practice that they do over there in Asia.
We Americans and Canadians are more forward-looking, usually.
We're about the now.
We're about tomorrow.
We're about our upcoming trip.
We're about the new things that we're doing.
We're about ourselves.
We're a little bit proud of this tendency, being the now people.
But I'm thinking of the passing of Robert Aitken Roshi and his great and steady effort in practice over all those years.
The story of how he started practice is kind of amazing.
That's a little digression.
Do you know this story?
I think he had maybe finished his bachelor's.
He was young, in his early twenties, and he got a job in Japan right before the war broke out, doing some kind of labor or something.
I'm not sure how he got this job.
He was in Japan when the war broke out, and so he got interned.
Somebody in the internment camp gave him a copy of this book.
I forget the title right now.
It's R.H.
Blythe, an R.H.
Blythe book.
*Zen and Western Literature*.
It was an examination of Western literature from a [unclear: "central"] perspective.
Exactly.
Someone gave him this book, and now suddenly he had a lot of time to read.
He read it from cover to cover several times, and he says in one of his memoirs or something that it really changed the way he was feeling about his life.
It made it much easier to be in the camp.
It was just kind of gross in the thinking in this book.
Then they transferred camps, and who's in his cell?
R.H.
Blythe.
They got to spend like a year and a half talking about this in the camp.
That's how he got interested in Zen.
After the war, he went back to America and then came back again to Japan, and he ended up studying Zen in Japan through most of the 1950s.
It just goes on from there, very steadily finding ways to practice, and there weren't too many practice opportunities in the late fifties.
He was in L.A. working in a bookstore, and there was exactly one Japanese Zen priest in all of L.A.
So he studied with him.
It's a little amazing, though.

It also strikes me as a great example of the Chinese story style, where bad things happen to the character and then it turns out for other reasons to be a good thing, and a good thing happens and turns out to be a bad thing, and it goes on and on like that.
A war breaks out, and you're locked up, and it turns out to be the most important thing that ever happened in your life.
Anyway, thinking about all this, and also thinking about our time in Japan, I'm thinking of standing in the Abbots' graveyard at Suzuki Shunryu [unclear: "Orochi's"] family temple, Rinso-in.
Up on the hill a little bit, above the main buildings, is a small graveyard, and it's just for the abbots.
They each have a marker that looks like a stupa.
There are fifty-three or something abbots of Rinso-in there, which doesn't seem like quite enough.
Maybe some got skipped or something, because the temple's been there for 500 years.
We went up there and did a memorial service for Suzuki [unclear: "Orochi"], who's the Japanese priest who founded the San Francisco Zen Center, also in the late 50s.
Conducting the memorial service were his son, Suzuki [unclear: "Huitz"], now in his late 70s himself, and his grandson, Suzuki Shungo, mid-30s, both Soto Zen priests.

The temple's been there for 500 years, and we're chanting in the way that they've been chanting for a pretty long time, burning incense that's mingling with the incense burned there for hundreds and hundreds of years.
Then I was also thinking of when we were at Ehiji Monastery, which is one of the sort of second biggest things.
Soji's a little bigger.
It's the second biggest training monastery for Japanese Soto Zen.
It wasn't actually that big, smaller than a university, a small college, I guess.
But anyway, the day we were there, they were doing a memorial service as part of the morning practice.
Some of that morning practice was going to include [unclear: "Norman"], which is why we were there.
It was a memorial service for Rujing, who's Dogen's teacher in China.
They told us, and it's probably true, that they've done a memorial service for Rujing on that day of the year, every year, since the monastery was founded just about 800 years ago.
Of course, none of these people has ever met Dogen's teacher, Rujing.
No one at the memorial service at [unclear: "Urinsuin"] had met the 40 or 50 past abbots.
A couple of people there had met one of them.
In fact, Suzuki Shungo, the 30-something priest who was there, had never met his grandfather, actually.
And yet there was some deep connection going on, like a personal connection.
It doesn't really matter if they had met.
It didn't really matter whether they had personally had some interaction or knew some story or had something to sort of hang their hat on.
I doubt any of the monks at Eiji [unclear: "like Pickley"] knew a single teaching of Rujing or anything like that.
It's just that he is an ancestor.
It wasn't like they were making something up, either.
There's a deep sense of connection, a non-personal or maybe a transpersonal connection.
Actually, it can also be that there's a personal connection which is not so great.
Suzuki [unclear: "who eats"], sort of our Suzuki Roshi's... now I'm having trouble with what to call these people.
I can't really say Suzuki Roshi, actually, because that's what we've always said about Suzuki Shunryu, but Suzuki [unclear: "who eats"] is actually Suzuki Roshi.
So names are trouble.
Anyway, he made a point of telling us that even though he understands that his father was a really important and great Zen teacher in America, he was actually a pretty crappy father.
He said that people had more than one side, and one of those sides could be quite ugly and unenlightened.
And yet there was no holding back in his conduct of the memorial service for his father.
He was right there chanting with his whole body, offering incense with his whole heart.

So this connection and reverence with ancestors, spiritual ancestors or family ancestors, and Jeff's always reminding me of the old people in our land here who feel this same kind of connection to ancestors.
This connection is not predicated on conventional relationship or opinion or preference.

It's some kind of deep connection, some sort of transcendent respect, a kind of opening to something larger than the personal or the self, some way of touching the universal stream of human life and non-human life.

So now I'm feeling like Aitken Roshi's passing away right after this trip to Asia, where we learned a little bit about these things, and of course these things are things one can only learn experientially, that he died so soon after that feels like an important teaching that he was offering us.
Here is one of our ancestors, worthy of our deepest respect and reverence, whether we ever met him or not, or even if we never do get around to reading any of his books.
I take back the other thing I said: don't read his books unless you want to.
He's still your ancestor.
Wouldn't it be a shame, [unclear: "for a criminal almost"], to not fully commit ourselves to carrying forth his Zen spirit and offering that to the next generation?
There's a lot of ways one might do that.

One thing that came to me reading these blog postings is that one way of honoring this, our ancestor Aitken Roshi, here in our pretty shallowly rooted Buddhist practice in America, [unclear: "to our little shell"], one way we could do this is to follow his suggestion to count the breath.
It's a practice I used to do for a long time, actually.
A long time before any [unclear: "futures"] ever told me there is any other choices, actually.
I thought that was the only kind of practice there was in Zen.
If you don't know this practice, it's very simple, which does not mean it's not completely profound and important.
It's an embodied practice like all meditation practice is, not a mental discipline.
Feeling the breath fully in the body, body open and upright, emphasizing the breathing in the belly, maybe a little bit artificial at first and then just naturally letting it be.
Then just notice exhalation.
Exhalation.
And count to oneself a one.
The next exhalation is a two, and so on, up to ten.
If one gets distracted, return to one.
Sometimes in Soto Zen, we think of this as sort of a beginner's practice, and we suggest that new people practice this, which is very helpful.
It can appear to be a sort of concentration practice that will settle people in for a year or ten years.
I did nothing but breath counting for at least ten years.
After a while I got really mechanical about it.
I went and talked to somebody about it and she suggested we'll count backwards.
So for another three or four years I counted backwards, ten down to one.
So you can try that.
If you want to join me in this, you don't have to.
We could take this up on our trip together, to see if we could do this wholeheartedly, not as a sort of lesser practice or a beginner practice, but as a complete practice.

And to see if we can a little bit short-circuit our strong tendency to think of everything we do as having a sort of linear trajectory: starting here, getting a little better, getting a little better.
Oops, step back.
Getting better, getting better, getting better, off into the horizon.
Maybe meditation practice does not progress in a linear way.
Maybe it's not a matter of getting better at something.
And if we do have to impose some sort of progression on our practice, maybe circular would be more helpful than linear.
Coming around again and coming around again.
As we study our mind, I think we can relate to that.
Same damn stuff, right?
But is it the same?
Or is it just coming around again?
And you can face it fresh.
Because we're never doing the same thing.
No two breaths in our whole life are the same.
But we're never exactly doing something new or different either.
Lately also I've been developing, this came to me during meditation, I have to admit, a sort of theory, or a way that we might look at meditation.
Of course meditation is sort of beyond conceptualization, but we seem to need some concepts and some techniques.

So here's a sort of three-legged stool we could use to think about how we're practicing meditation, and we could, if we wanted, see how this applies to breath counting practice if we take that up, or any kind of practice we're doing.
I think I made these three categories up, but they're based on traditional [unclear: "topologies"] of meditation and on my experience.
So here, according to me, are the three essential aspects of meditation.
I just want to invite you, if you want, on this weekend retreat, to explore these or forget all about them.
The first of the three aspects of meditation is establishing.
This is the obvious and overt doing part of meditation: establishing and maintaining the container of meditation practice.
Working with our posture is establishing.
Taking up a technique deliberately, like breath counting, is establishing.
Of course establishing is quite critical.
If we don't establish some container for practice with some care, practice just doesn't really function.
Good intentions without establishing are very weak.
Over-emphasizing establishing at the expense of the other two aspects of meditation, which I'll get to, results in a practice that is really stiff, really rigid, trying too hard.
Practice that's only establishing can be sort of self-defeating, and ultimately your own suffering sort of beats you back from that course.
So you don't have to worry too much.
It's sort of self-correcting, and we can see that in all of our activities: too much trying to do it, that's only establishing, trying to establish something, trying to do something.
The second aspect of meditation is releasing.
Releasing is letting go.
It's the non-doing of meditation practice.
The space in the body.
Opening the heart.
Releasing is letting thoughts come and go without engaging or embroidering on them.
Releasing is soft.
Releasing is peaceful and free.
Releasing is more possible, actually, than our habitual mind tells us it is.
Releasing is maybe like the lubrication of meditation.
And the value of releasing is pretty clear.
As with establishing, if our practice is too much in that basket, it doesn't function well.
We're drifting and loose like a cloud that never finds its way home.
We get fuzzy, a little confused.
And true releasing seems to really need the strength and discipline of establishing to allow it free functioning.
The third aspect of meditation, after establishing and releasing, is inquiring.
Asking the deepest human questions without expecting answers.
Inquiring is turning towards our experience without judgment or complaint, openly, curiously.
Inquiring is curiosity, curiosity about this rich and confusing human life.
There are some techniques from the establishing camp that can help to develop inquiring, like holding in the mind a Dharma phrase or a question; one could breathe with a question like "What is it?"
That can be helpful.
But ultimately, inquiring floats free from any technique.
Inquiring is really the path to wisdom and discovery.
It gives our practice life.
But of course too much energy here is also a problem.
If we lean into inquiry, our practice becomes goal-driven and narrow.
We get upset.
We're not figuring anything out.
We feel dumber than when we started.
But gentle inquiry in the context of releasing and held by the container of establishing is basically enlightening, I guess is the appropriate word.
So if that rubric is helpful to you, please use it.
Don't worry about it.
Establishing, releasing, inquiring.
One could run through that in the first few minutes of every meditation period, just touch base with those three aspects of our effort or non-effort.
Since I thought of all this, I myself have been really trying to do breath counting practice with that broad framework.
It might be we understood breath counting practice originally as only establishing, later to be let go of so that we can release and inquire.
But actually any technique does include all three of these aspects.
The beauty of breath counting practice, actually, to make a little more of a [unclear: "sell"], I guess, is just how radically honest it is.
There's all kinds of less structured practices where you can drift along pretty happily for a long time.
But if you're breath counting and you can't remember what number you're on, it's pretty clear.
And if you're breath counting and it's very rigid and mechanical, that's also pretty clear.

To just use that road because Aitken Roshi, our ancestor, recommends it, to follow in his footsteps for months or years, just settling with breath counting, releasing into the radical openness of our life.
Our time is short.
What is birth and death?
Can the numbers be soft as they release into the quiet?
They merge us with the mountains that are constantly walking.
I'll close with a few lines from the sutra.
I'll refrain from trying to say anything interpretive.
Here's what Dogen tells us, that we'll read on the trail, chant on the trail.
*Mountains and waters right now are the actualization of the ancient Buddha way.

Each abiding in its phenomenal expression realizes completeness because mountains and waters have been active since before the empty Aeon, and they are alive at this moment because they have been the self since [unclear: "before former rose"].
They are emancipation and realization because mountains are high and broad.
The way of riding the clouds is always reached in the mountains.
The inconceivable power of soaring in the wind comes freely from the mountains.*
*And priest Daokai of Mount Furong said to the assembly, "The green mountains are always walking."
Mountains do not lack the qualities of mountains.
They always abide in ease.
They always walk.
You should examine in detail this quality of the mountains walking.
Mountains walking is just like human walking.
Accordingly, do not doubt mountains walking even though it does not look the same as human walking.
The Buddha ancestors' words point to walking.
This is a fundamental understanding.
You should penetrate these words.*
